title: 30x30 and the 'Paper Park' Problem
hook: The world pledged to protect 30% of the ocean by 2030. But a line on a map isn't protection — and much of what's been promised exists only on paper.
key_points: '30x30' is the global goal to protect 30% of land and sea by 2030, agreed under a UN biodiversity framework.
So far only about 10% of the ocean has formal protection, and progress is often measured by area alone.
A 'paper park' is protected in law but not in practice — little enforcement, funding, or real limits on harm.
Measuring conservation by square kilometers can reward easy designations over meaningful protection.
content_html: In 2022, governments meeting under a United Nations biodiversity framework set a headline target known as 30x30: protect 30% of the planet's land and ocean by the year 2030. It is a simple, memorable goal — and that simplicity is part of the problem. Roughly 10% of the ocean currently has some formal protection, and the most common way to track progress is to add up the area inside protected boundaries.
extra_html: Writing in The Conversation, marine scientists Kirsten Grorud-Colvert and Ana Spalding argue that area is a misleading yardstick. Many designated zones are "paper parks" — protected in law but with little funding, enforcement, or real restriction on fishing and other harm. A vast, weakly-guarded reserve can pad the numbers while a small, strictly enforced one does more good. The authors press for judging protection by what actually changes in the water — the rules, the enforcement, the recovery of marine life — not just the square kilometers drawn on a map. It is a general lesson about policy targets: a metric that is easy to count can quietly reward the appearance of action over the substance.

related.title: Environmental Governance
related.hook: How do you regulate something that ignores borders and belongs to no one? Environmental governance is the toolkit societies use to manage nature collectively.

related.title: The Tragedy of the Commons
related.hook: When everyone shares a resource but no one owns it, each person's rational choice can add up to collective ruin. That trap explains a huge slice of environmental politics.

related.title: Treaties & International Law
related.hook: If no world government can pass laws, how do nations bind themselves at all? Largely by agreeing to — treaties are the contracts that knit the international order together.

flashcards.back_html: A global pledge to protect 30% of the planet's land and ocean by 2030, adopted under a UN biodiversity framework.

choices.text: An area protected in law but lacking real enforcement or limits on harm
A park that exists only in historical records
A protected zone open only to scientists

flashcards.explanation_html: Paper parks count toward targets on paper while doing little on the water — the gap the authors warn about.

flashcards.prompt: Why do the authors say marine protection 'can't be judged by area alone'?

choices.text: Counting square kilometers can reward easy designations over real protection
Ocean area is impossible to measure accurately
Only land area counts under the 30x30 goal

flashcards.explanation_html: Area is a tempting but shallow metric: a huge weakly-protected zone can look better than a small, strictly enforced one. Quality matters too.
